claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is one of the deadliest human cancers with no clinically effective treatment options.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) is one of the deadliest human cancers with no clinically effective treatment options (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2020

claim: PDA is characterized by an intense fibroinflammatory stroma, poor vascularity, deregulated nutrient levels, and rich deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) components.
source: PDA is characterized by an intense fibroinflammatory stroma, poor vascularity, deregulated nutrient levels, and rich deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM) components.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about PDA characteristics

claim: Mutant Kras facilitates the rewiring of PDA metabolism to enable survival and proliferation in the nutrient austere tumor microenvironment.
source: To survive and proliferate in this nutrient austere tumor microenvironment (TME), the oncogenic driver in PDA, mutant Kras, facilitates the rewiring of PDA metabolism (Halbrook and Lyssiotis, 2017; Perera and Bardeesy, 2015; Ying et al., 2016; Kerk et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: Mutant Kras signaling results in upregulated expression of Gfpt1, which encodes GFAT1.
source: Signaling downstream of Kras results in upregulated expression of Gfpt1, which encodes glutamine-fructose 6-phosphate amidotransferase 1 (GFAT1).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Ying et al., 2012)

claim: The hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) is an evolutionarily conserved pathway that integrates glucose, glutamine, fatty acid, and nucleotide metabolism to generate UDP-GlcNAc.
source: The HBP is an evolutionarily conserved pathway that integrates glucose, glutamine, fatty acid, and nucleotide metabolism to generate the final product uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about the HBP

claim: UDP-GlcNAc is a crucial donor molecule for glycosylation and O-GlcNAcylation, two essential post-translational modifications required for cellular structure, signaling, and survival.
source: UDP-GlcNAc is a crucial donor molecule for glycosylation and O-GlcNAcylation, two essential post-translational modifications required for cellular structure, signaling, and survival (Akella et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Akella et al., 2019

claim: The HBP is the only pathway able to generate UDP-GlcNAc de novo.
source: The HBP is the only pathway able to generate UDP-GlcNAc de novo.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis

claim: The HBP functions as a nutrient sensing mechanism for available energy within a cell.
source: Because the HBP integrates nutrients from several major macromolecular classes to produce UDP-GlcNAc, it predictably functions as a nutrient sensing mechanism for available energy within a cell (Wellen et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wellen et al., 2010

claim: HBP activity is enhanced in numerous cancer subtypes to support tumor survival and growth.
source: Indeed, numerous studies across cancer subtypes have demonstrated how HBP activity is enhanced to support tumor survival and growth (Paszek et al., 2014; Akella et al., 2019; Walter et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2016) and even immune evasion through alteration of extracellular glycosylation content (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: PDA cells fuel their aberrant metabolic programs through nutrient scavenging.
source: A compendium of studies during the last decade have revealed that PDA cells fuel their aberrant metabolic programs through nutrient scavenging (Ying et al., 2012; Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2011; Davidson et al., 2017; Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: PDA cells participate in metabolic crosstalk and nutrient acquisition with cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs).
source: Further, PDA cells also participate in metabolic crosstalk and nutrient acquisition with non-cancerous cells in the TME, such as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) (Sousa et al., 2016; Dalin et al., 2019; Halbrook et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020; Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: PDA cells can directly obtain nutrients from the CAF-derived ECM, such as collagen.
source: A notable example is the observation that PDA cells can directly obtain nutrients from the CAF-derived ECM, such as collagen (Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olivares et al., 2017

claim: Hyaluronic acid (HA) is a hydrophilic glycosaminoglycan that is ubiquitously present in human tissue, especially in skin, connective tissue, and joints.
source: A major structural component of the TME is hyaluronic acid (HA), a hydrophilic glycosaminoglycan. HA is ubiquitously present in human tissue, especially in skin, connective tissue, and joints, and it is richly abundant in pancreatic tumors (Theocharis et al., 2000).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and citation to Theocharis et al., 2000

claim: HA is richly abundant in pancreatic tumors.
source: HA is ubiquitously present in human tissue, especially in skin, connective tissue, and joints, and it is richly abundant in pancreatic tumors (Theocharis et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Theocharis et al., 2000

claim: HA is thought to be primarily deposited by CAFs and, to some extent, by PDA cells.
source: HA is thought to be primarily deposited by CAFs and, to some extent, by PDA cells (Goossens et al., 2019; Mahlbacher et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goossens et al., 2019 and Mahlbacher et al., 1992

claim: HA avidly retains water, which is responsible for both its lubricating properties and, in PDA tumors, the supraphysiological pressure that impairs vascularity and limits drug penetrance.
source: HA avidly retains water, which is responsible for both its lubricating properties and, in PDA tumors, the supraphysiological pressure that impairs vascularity and limits drug penetrance (Jacobetz et al., 2013; Provenzano et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacobetz et al., 2013 and Provenzano et al., 2012

claim: HA is a carbohydrate polymer whose monomeric unit is a disaccharide of glucuronic acid and N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc).
source: This is surprising given that HA is a carbohydrate polymer whose monomeric unit is a disaccharide of glucuronic acid and N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about HA structure

claim: GFAT1 catalyzes the reaction that generates glucosamine 6-phosphate and glutamate from fructose 6-phosphate and glutamine.
source: GFAT1 catalyzes the reaction that generates glucosamine 6-phosphate and glutamate from fructose 6-phosphate and glutamine (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by text description and Figure 1A showing the HBP pathway

claim: PDA cells are dependent on glutamine anaplerosis for proliferation.
source: In another previous study we demonstrated that PDA cells are dependent on glutamine anaplerosis for proliferation (Son et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Son et al., 2013

claim: GFAT1 knockout completely blocked proliferation of human PDA cell lines in vitro and led to cell death.
source: Here, we genetically ablated GFAT1 in human PDA cell lines, which completely blocked proliferation in vitro and led to cell death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: GFAT1 knockout did not preclude the growth of human tumor xenografts in mice.
source: In contrast, GFAT1 knockout did not preclude the growth of human tumor xenografts in mice, suggesting that cancer cells can maintain fidelity of glycosylation precursor pools by scavenging nutrients from the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Cancer cells can maintain fidelity of glycosylation precursor pools by scavenging nutrients from the tumor microenvironment.
source: In contrast, GFAT1 knockout did not preclude the growth of human tumor xenografts in mice, suggesting that cancer cells can maintain fidelity of glycosylation precursor pools by scavenging nutrients from the tumor microenvironment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GFAT1 knockout tumors grow in vivo but not in vitro

claim: Hyaluronic acid (HA) can bypass GFAT1 to refuel the HBP via the GlcNAc salvage pathway.
source: We found that hyaluronic acid (HA), an abundant carbohydrate polymer in pancreatic tumors composed of repeating N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc) and glucuronic acid sugars, can bypass GFAT1 to refuel the HBP via the GlcNAc salvage pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: HA can serve as a nutrient fueling PDA metabolism beyond its previously appreciated structural and signaling roles.
source: Together, these data show HA can serve as a nutrient fueling PDA metabolism beyond its previously appreciated structural and signaling roles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: GFAT1 knockout was validated in TU8988T, MiaPaca2, and HPAC cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: Western blot of GFAT1 and loading control VINCULIN (VNC) from validated CRISPR/Cas9 knockout TU8988T, MiaPaca2, and HPAC clones and their control (non-targeted sgRNA).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1B

claim: GFAT1 knockout abolished colony formation in all three PDA cell lines in vitro.
source: Using our genomically sequenced and bona fide GFAT1 knockout clonal lines, we found that GFAT1 knockout led to an abolishment of colony formation (Figure 1C) and potently impaired proliferation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) in all three PDA cell lines in vitro.
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 1C

claim: GFAT1 knockout potently impaired proliferation in all three PDA cell lines in vitro.
source: Using our genomically sequenced and bona fide GFAT1 knockout clonal lines, we found that GFAT1 knockout led to an abolishment of colony formation (Figure 1C) and potently impaired proliferation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) in all three PDA cell lines in vitro.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 1D

claim: GFAT1 knockout clonal lines readily formed tumors comparable to wildtype counterparts when implanted into the flanks of immunocompromised mice.
source: Surprisingly, when either the pooled or the clonal knockout lines were implanted into the flanks of immunocompromised mice, they readily formed tumors that were comparable to their wildtype counterparts in terms of weight and volume (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data in Figure 1E and F

claim: GFAT1 knockout clonal lines grown orthotopically in the pancreas were smaller than wildtype tumors at endpoint.
source: Of note, while clearly capable of forming tumors, the GFAT1 knockout clonal lines grown in the pancreas were smaller than the wildtype tumors at endpoint.
evidence: Supported by tumor growth data in Figure 1G

claim: Conditioned media from patient-derived CAFs resulted in a significant, albeit modest, rescue in colony formation of GFAT1 knockout clones.
source: When GFAT1 knockout clones were incubated in patient-derived CAF CM, we observed a significant, albeit modest, rescue in colony formation (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 2A and B

claim: Conditioned media from wildtype TU8988T cells resulted in a more robust, dose-dependent rescue of colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we observed a more robust, dose-dependent rescue of colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells with CM from wildtype TU8988T cells (Figure 2C–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 2C-F

claim: Conditioned media from wildtype HPAC and MiaPaCa2 cells was able to partially rescue proliferation of a subset of GFAT1 knockout clones.
source: Similarly, CM from wildtype HPAC and MiaPaCa2 cells was able to partially rescue proliferation of a subset of GFAT1 knockout clones (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data in Figure 2G

claim: Both CAF and PDA conditioned media retained the ability to support colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells after boiling or repeated cycles of freezing and thawing.
source: To begin to identify the rescue factors in the CM, we subjected the CM to boiling or repeated cycles of freezing and thawing (F/T). In each of these conditions, both the CAF and the PDA CM retained the ability to support colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 2A-D

claim: The rescue factor(s) in conditioned media do not require tertiary structure.
source: These results suggested the relevant factor(s) did not require tertiary structure.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that boiling and freeze-thaw do not eliminate rescue activity

claim: The rescue activity of conditioned media was dose dependent.
source: Additionally, we observed that the rescue activity of the CM was dose dependent (Figure 2E–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 2E-G

claim: Millimolar quantities of GlcNAc (>0.625 mM) were required to rescue colony formation of GFAT1 knockout PDA cells.
source: GlcNAc dose response curves demonstrated that millimolar quantities of GlcNAc (>0.625 mM) were required to rescue colony formation of GFAT1 knockout PDA cells (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 2H

claim: GlcNAc in conditioned media was in the low micromolar range, several orders of magnitude below the millimolar doses of exogenous GlcNAc required to maintain proliferation.
source: By contrast, LC-MS/MS quantification of GlcNAc in the CM revealed that it was in the low micromolar range (Figure 2I), several orders of magnitude below the millimolar doses of exogenous GlcNAc required to maintain proliferation (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 2I and dose-response data in Figure 2H

claim: Free GlcNAc was not the relevant molecule in conditioned media mediating rescue of GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: These results illustrated that free GlcNAc was not the relevant molecule in the CM mediating rescue.
evidence: Inferred from the discrepancy between GlcNAc concentration in CM and the concentration required for rescue

claim: Necrotic cellular debris from FL5.12 cells was unable to rescue GFAT1 knockout across the cell line panel.
source: Necrotic cell debris was unable to rescue GFAT1 knockout across our cell line panel (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: High-dose heparin was not able to rescue colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: Next, we tested if glycosaminoglycan carbohydrate polymers could mediate rescue of GFAT1 knockout, in a matter akin to CM. High-dose heparin was not able to rescue colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F

claim: 78 kDa HA provided a modest but significant rescue of colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: In contrast, 78 kDa HA provided a modest but significant rescue (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 3A and B

claim: Low molecular weight HA (78 kDa) was able to rescue total proteome O-GlcNAc levels in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: Consistent with the rescue of colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells, LMW HA (78 kDa) was also able to rescue total proteome O-GlcNAc levels, as assessed by western blot (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 3C-E

claim: PDA cell lines exhibited considerable macropinocytosis activity.
source: However, in PDA, mutant Kras drives macropinocytosis (Commisso et al., 2013), and quantitation of macropinocytotic activity with a fluorescent dextran-based assay revealed that our three PDA cell lines exhibited considerable macropinocytosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by macropinocytosis assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: GFAT1-proficient and GFAT1 knockout cells readily take up HA.
source: Similarly, following HA uptake using a fluorescently conjugated HA (HA-FITC) revealed GFAT1-proficient and GFAT1 knockout cells readily take up HA (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by HA-FITC uptake data in Figure 3F

claim: Utilizing hyaluronidase to break down LMW HA enhanced the rescue of colony formation in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, utilizing hyaluronidase to break down LMW HA enhanced the rescue of colony formation (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 3G

claim: HA-mediated rescue of proliferation was considerably higher for o-HA (5 kDa) than for LMW HA (60 kDa), and comparable to PDA CM.
source: This analysis revealed that HA-mediated rescue, as measured through proliferation quantification, was considerably higher for o-HA than for LMW HA, and comparable to PDA CM (Figure 3H, I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data in Figure 3H and I

claim: CAF CM contained considerably more HA than PDA CM.
source: CAF CM contained considerably more HA than PDA CM, consistent with the known role for fibroblasts in the production of HA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by HA ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F

claim: The lower limit of detection for the HA ELISA was ~50 kDa HA.
source: However, we found that the lower limit of detection for the ELISA was ~50 kDA HA.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E

claim: 4-MU dose dependently blocked HA release into conditioned media.
source: Indeed, we demonstrated that 4-MU dose dependently blocked HA release into CM (Figure 4A) while also exhibiting proliferative defects at the highest concentration tested (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: Supported by HA quantification data in Figure 4A

claim: The reduction in HA content in conditioned media from 4-MU-treated wildtype PDA cells paralleled the decrease in CM rescue activity in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: Application of CM from 4-MU-treated wildtype PDA cells in GFAT1 rescue assays revealed that the reduction in HA content paralleled the decrease in CM rescue activity in GFAT1 knockout cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data in Figure 4E

claim: HA is the relevant factor mediating the rescue activity of PDA CM in GFAT1 knockout cells.
source: These collective in vitro studies illustrate that HA can rescue the proliferation of GFAT1 knockout cells and strongly suggest that HA is the relevant factor mediating the rescue activity of PDA CM.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental data showing HA rescue and 4-MU inhibition

claim: HA is available to PDA tumors in subcutaneous and orthotopic models.
source: First, these data demonstrate that HA is available to PDA tumors in these models.
evidence: Supported by HABP staining data in Figure 4F-H

claim: There was more HA in subcutaneous tumors than orthotopic tumors.
source: Blinded scoring using a 0–3 scale (Figure 4G) revealed more HA in the subcutaneous than orthotopic setting (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by HABP staining quantification in Figure 4H

claim: There was a marked reduction in HABP staining in orthotopic GFAT1 knockout tumors compared to wildtype.
source: Tumor genotype did not influence HABP levels in the subcutaneous model, whereas there was a marked reduction in HABP staining in the orthotopic GFAT1 knockout tumors (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by HABP staining quantification in Figure 4H

claim: The difference in growth of GFAT1 knockout tumors in the orthotopic model compared to subcutaneous may result from less HA availability.
source: Further, they suggest that the difference in growth of GFAT1 knockout tumors in the orthotopic model compared to subcutaneous, as observed in Figure 1E–G, may result from less HA availability.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between HA levels and tumor growth differences

claim: Knockout of NAGK in parental TU8988T and MiaPaCa2 cell lines had no impact on colony formation.
source: Knockout of NAGK in parental TU8988T and MiaPaCa2 cell lines had no impact on colony formation, while reducing the colony-forming capacity of HPAC cells (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 5B and C

claim: Knockout of NAGK reduced the colony-forming capacity of HPAC cells.
source: Knockout of NAGK in parental TU8988T and MiaPaCa2 cell lines had no impact on colony formation, while reducing the colony-forming capacity of HPAC cells (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 5B and C

claim: The impact of NAGK knockout on colony formation correlated with the elevated expression of NAGK in wildtype HPAC cells.
source: These results correlated with the elevated expression of NAGK in wildtype HPAC cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5D

claim: NAGK knockout did not result in up-regulation of GFAT1.
source: Of note, NAGK knockout did not result in up-regulation of GFAT1 (Figure 5A), which could have suggested a compensatory metabolic rewiring.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 5A

claim: GalNAc can rescue GFAT1 knockout clones.
source: The GalNAc dose response for GFAT1 knockout clones was comparable to that of GlcNAc (Figure 2H), demonstrating that they are indeed viable in GalNAc (Figure 5F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Supported by colony formation assay data in Figure 5F

claim: LMW HA, o-HA, and PDA CM were unable to rescue GFAT1/NAGK double knockout lines.
source: In stark contrast to the GFAT1 knockout line, LMW HA, o-HA, and PDA CM were unable to rescue GFAT1/NAGK double knockout lines (Figure 5H–K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data in Figure 5H-K

claim: HA or PDA CM rescue of GFAT1 knockout cells restores UDP-GlcNAc pools and proteome O-GlcNAcylation, and this was blocked by knocking out NAGK.
source: HA or PDA CM rescue of GFAT1 knockout cells restores UDP-GlcNAc pools and proteome O-GlcNAcylation, and this was blocked by knocking out NAGK (Figure 5L and M and Figure 5—figure supplement 1K-N).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS and western blot data in Figure 5L and M

claim: HA rescue requires NAGK and the GlcNAc salvage pathway.
source: These results illustrate that HA rescue requires NAGK and the GlcNAc salvage pathway, consistent with the idea that HA-derived GlcNAc fuels UDP-GlcNAc biosynthesis upon GFAT1 knockout.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NAGK knockout blocks HA rescue

claim: HA regulates PDA metabolism by refueling the HBP via the GlcNAc salvage pathway to support PDA survival and proliferation.
source: Altogether, our data implicate HA as a novel nutrient for PDA, where HA regulates PDA metabolism by refueling the HBP via the GlcNAc salvage pathway. This supports PDA survival and proliferation (Figure 5N).
evidence: Supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: GFAT2 was neither regulated by mutant KRAS nor basally expressed in the models employed in this study.
source: We did not pursue GFAT2 in this study because it was neither regulated by mutant KRAS nor basally expressed in the models employed herein.
evidence: Statement about experimental design and rationale

claim: Pan glutamine-deamidase inhibitors (e.g. azaserine and 6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine) have demonstrated anti-tumor activity in vitro and in vivo in PDA and other cancers.
source: Several pan glutamine-deamidase inhibitors (e.g. azaserine and 6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine), which potently suppress GFAT activity, have demonstrated anti-tumor activity in vitro and in vivo in PDA and other cancers (Leone et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leone et al., 2019 and Sharma et al., 2020

claim: In tumors and tumor interstitial fluid, there is a significantly elevated level of low molecular weight (LMW; 10–250 kDa) and oligo-HA (o-HA; <10 kDa).
source: However, in tumors and tumor interstitial fluid, there is a significantly elevated level of low molecular weight (LMW; 10–250 kDa) and oligo-HA (o-HA; <10 kDa) (Schmaus et al., 2014; Lv et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmaus et al., 2014 and Lv et al., 2007

claim: In non-pathological settings, newly synthesized HA is predominantly high molecular weight (HMW; >1000 kDa).
source: In non-pathological settings, newly synthesized HA is predominantly high molecular weight (HMW; >1000 kDa) (Monslow et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Monslow et al., 2015

claim: Cancer cells have been reported to uptake HA via macropinocytosis.
source: Cancer cells have been reported to uptake HA via macropinocytosis (Greyner et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greyner et al., 2010

claim: Mutant Kras drives macropinocytosis in PDA.
source: However, in PDA, mutant Kras drives macropinocytosis (Commisso et al., 2013), and quantitation of macropinocytotic activity with a fluorescent dextran-based assay revealed that our three PDA cell lines exhibited considerable macropinocytosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by citation to Commisso et al., 2013

claim: The rate limiting step for HA utilization is not HA entry into cells, but rather, the cleavage of HA into smaller fragments.
source: This led us to hypothesize that the rate limiting step is not HA entry into cells, but rather, the cleavage of HA into smaller fragments.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hyaluronidase treatment enhances rescue

claim: Hyaluronidase has been reported to directly impact cellular metabolism.
source: Of note, hyaluronidase was heat-inactivated after it was used to cleave HA (i.e. before its application to GFAT1 knockout cells; Figure 3—figure supplement 1I), as hyaluronidase has been reported to directly impact cellular metabolism (Sullivan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2018

claim: HA is produced by the family of HA synthases, which can be inhibited in vitro with the tool compound 4-methylumbelliferone (4-MU).
source: HA is produced by the family of HA synthases, which can be inhibited in vitro with the tool compound 4-methylumbelliferone (4-MU) (Nagy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nagy et al., 2015

claim: The role of HA in GFAT1 knockout PDA cells is likely independent of its structural and signaling functions.
source: The role of HA in GFAT1 knockout PDA cells described herein is likely independent of its structural and signaling functions, given that we observe considerably greater rescue with o-HA (Figure 3H, I), a form of HA that is not traditionally considered for these purposes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that o-HA provides greater rescue than LMW HA

claim: HA can activate cell-cell contact-mediated signal transduction through CD44 and/or receptor for HA-mediated motility (RHAMM).
source: For example, HA can activate cell-cell contact-mediated signal transduction through CD44 and/or receptor for HA-mediated motility (Misra et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Misra et al., 2015

claim: The signaling activity/function of HA depends on its molecular weight.
source: The signaling activity/function of HA depends on its MW (Toole, 2004; Vigetti et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Toole, 2004 and Vigetti et al., 2014

claim: Breakdown of the HA matrix with hyaluronidase enabled the interaction between growth factors and growth factor receptors, promoting glucose metabolism, cellular proliferation, and migration.
source: Similarly, a recent study illustrated that breakdown of the HA matrix with hyaluronidase enabled the interaction between growth factors and growth factor receptors (Sullivan et al., 2018). This promoted glucose metabolism, cellular proliferation, and migration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2018

claim: NAGK knockout in PDA impairs tumor growth in vivo, while only exhibiting a modest impact on cellular proliferation in vitro.
source: Indeed, a recent study demonstrated that NAGK knockout in PDA impairs tumor growth in vivo, while only exhibiting a modest impact on cellular proliferation in vitro (Campbell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2021

claim: NAGK may be an attractive therapeutic target for PDA.
source: Additionally, our study suggests that NAGK, through which HA-mediated GlcNAc presumably refuels the HBP in vivo, may be an attractive therapeutic target for PDA.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the experimental findings

claim: The GlcNAc salvage pathway is used to fill UDP-GlcNAc pools with HA-derived GlcNAc.
source: These results are consistent with our observations that the GlcNAc salvage pathway is used to fill UDP-GlcNAc pools with HA-derived GlcNAc (Figure 5N).
evidence: Supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: HA retains water and acts as a cushioning agent in tissue homeostasis and biomechanical integrity.
source: Due to its extremely hydrophilic nature, HA retains water and acts as a cushioning agent in tissue homeostasis and biomechanical integrity (Toole, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Toole, 2004

claim: HA is a predominant component of the PDA tumor microenvironment, and its water-retaining property is one of the main drivers of the supraphysiological intratumoral pressure.
source: In PDA, HA is a predominant component of the TME, and its water-retaining property is one of the main drivers of the supraphysiological intratumoral pressure (DuFort and DelGiorno, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to DuFort and DelGiorno, 2016

claim: Intratumoral pressure in PDA can exceed 10-fold that observed in the normal pancreas, causing tumor vasculature to collapse.
source: This pressure can exceed 10-fold that observed in the normal pancreas, and, as a result, tumor vasculature collapses (Provenzano et al., 2012; DuFort et al., 2016; Jacobetz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Provenzano et al., 2012, DuFort et al., 2016, and Jacobetz et al., 2013

claim: Limited access to circulation impairs nutrient and oxygen delivery and is a critical impediment to tumoral drug delivery.
source: The limited access to circulation impairs nutrient and oxygen delivery, and it has been proposed that this is a critical impediment to tumoral drug delivery (Olive et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olive et al., 2009

claim: In animal models, breakdown of the HA matrix with PEGPH20 reduces intratumoral pressure, restores circulation, facilitates drug delivery, and improves response to chemotherapy.
source: Indeed, in animal models, breakdown of the HA matrix with a therapeutic hyaluronidase (PEGPH20) reduces intratumoral pressure, restores circulation, which facilitates drug delivery, and thereby improves response to chemotherapy (Provenzano et al., 2012; Jacobetz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Provenzano et al., 2012 and Jacobetz et al., 2013

claim: PEGPH20 did not extend PDA patient survival in clinical trials.
source: Despite the successes in the preclinical models, PEGPH20 did not extend PDA patient survival (Van Cutsem et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Cutsem et al., 2020

claim: The HA matrix may be necessary to restrain tumor dissemination.
source: For example, the HA matrix may be necessary to restrain tumor dissemination, as was shown for CAF depletion studies in PDA (Helms et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2014; Özdemir et al., 2015; Rhim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Helms et al., 2020, Lee et al., 2014, Özdemir et al., 2015, and Rhim et al., 2014

claim: The benefits afforded by enhanced drug penetration facilitated by PEGPH20 may be negated by enhanced tumor dissemination.
source: Thus, the benefits afforded by enhanced drug penetration facilitated by PEGPH20 may be negated by this side effect.
evidence: Speculative statement based on prior observations

claim: HA degradation may enhance tumor metabolism and growth through growth factor signaling-dependent and signaling-independent pathways.
source: Along these lines, HA degradation may also enhance tumor metabolism and growth. This could occur through growth factor signaling-dependent (Sullivan et al., 2018) as well as signaling-independent pathways, like the GlcNAc salvage pathway described herein.

claim: Reduction in the HA content of tumors facilitates T cell invasion.
